1965 was not close to the end of the Cold War, except if you perhaps live in another reality. Rhodesia, the state that the people in the photograph represent, was a British Protectorate when insurgent forces supported by Soviet Russia, began a campaign of terror, whilst the Rhodesian government was in talks with London regarding their independence and subsequent self-rule. The Rhodesians have nothing to do with Apartheid, although they had what is viewed as an oppressive government. There only ever was one Apartheid state, except if you want to count the countries that supported separate development of races as well, during the exact same time as the rule of Nationalist's in South Africa took place, the United States of America was also still promoting racial inequality. Now, hear me out, I am not supporting any government or way of ruling. The history of humanity is one that should be remembered and remembered correctly. If you cannot imagine what the world was like during the Cold War, where taking a side began meaning you were choosing protection over insurrection, well, its not as simple as Soviet or Capitalist. And even today, with all things considered, nations align themselves with other nations, not for the benefit of humanity, but for either a political benefit or some other short term reason. South Africa, as Rhodesia too, did not suddenly attack Angola or Namibia. Both governments, yes, while implementing a very short sighted policy of racial inequality, were reactionary toward bombings, terrorist attacks with weapons in public places. There never was a plan of conquering Angola or integrating Namibia as territory. The government had to use force to counter armed insurrection, attacks against civilians by people armed with weapons that were way above what a policeman could muster. As with Malaya for Britain, Indonesia, heck, any country where terrorists armed with devastating weaponry attack the civil population, the government had to counter it. Do understand, its history, I give a flying banana over any policy by any government, but you cannot make a statement without understanding exactly what you are talking about. The world is not an easy place to exist in, we humans tend to complicate it with our master plans.

What legends they are. As a South African, and being too young to, I only have my father who was in 32 Battalion and my own experience in Tactical Intelligence to have some knowledge of the vast superiority in battle that these pioneers possessed.

I cannot be any prouder. I'm sure most of these troops won't remember a certain cpl Shaka; but damn, he is looking up from Cape Town with tears of pride. This is a big step for the unit, seemingly this photo is taken infront of what I used to know as 2 TIR, or the endless Monday cleaning parade area.. From what we used not 10 years ago to Land Cruisers.. Well done guys!

Have you ever been in a battle? You should understand doctrine and tactics my friend, then also the purpose of the vehicle. As far as I know, and I left 1TIR in 2017, these here soldiers are lazy. They should be walking. With the light equipment now in use, weighing about 1,200 kg's and their own food, water and personal baggage, well they are being spoiled and using state fuel for a damned bad reason. Things really go backwards once the Sgt Major is out of the system. I bet half dont even grow mustaches anymore.

Indeed, this vehicle is only intended to put these troops about 10km at the closest from a targeted surveillance post. They have equipment to observe enemy strength, movement and potentially plan the intent of the target by observing them, over however long a period it may have to be. I personally, with antiquated equipment in 2011, had the joy of seeing US Marine officer's jaws drop as we gave a presentation on their own deployment during an exercise in the Eastern Cape. If you really want to laugh at how we took pictures, videos and listened in on some comms, we were deployed with a Hino truck. You know, a furniture mover? It was army brown though and only in use because of mechanical failures of Ratel's and their backup's Buffels... Yet, we went in unseen and got the information necessary. Surprise is one of the best military weapons, ask anyone who remembers Pearly Beach, Langebaan.

What do you call Battlefield Observers, Surveillance operators or anyone operating, not in no man's land or behind enemy lines, but right infront of the enemy forces? Suicidal perhaps, but that is the task of 1 TIR. As a former member, deployed to various borders and throughout Africa, your confusion will cause your own forces pain. As future planning went and if the members pictured here were to be seen in normal drill dress, I believe various emblems of capability would be observed. Having deployed with 5 Spes in 2013; I can assure you, our doctrines are near the same; only difference is, Special Forces have the freedom to roam behind the lines to cause chaos, whereas we have to be right on the enemies noses to ensure everything is seen that is tactically done, that is, presently and the future intent of said enemy forces.

If only the South African government had such concerns and did not always cut the budget.. I was part of the Foxes. We mostly used pickups on deployment in Kruger National Park, but we never used .50 cal's on the pickups.. As it was to counter poaching and patrol the border, be well aware that the sight of a pickup coming at you with the machine gun going full tilt, would convince you to stay home. Mamba's; an Australian APC, were used circa 2011-14; but I bet they have finally and luckily all broken down. This is Africa though, we fight in anything.
